title: Care for poultry parent stock during production

lessons.title: Parent stock, biosecurity and daily checks
lessons.html:
What is parent stock?

Parent stock (also called breeders) are the hens and cockerels kept to produce fertile hatching eggs. These eggs go to a hatchery, and the chicks become the broilers or layers that other farms raise. One parent flock affects hundreds of thousands of chicks, so its health and care are very important. A disease in a breeder farm can spread to many farms through the eggs and chicks.

Biosecurity: keeping disease out

Breeder farms have strict biosecurity rules. Follow every rule, every time:

  • Shower in and change into clean farm clothes and boots before entering the production area.
  • Step through the footbath at each house door. Keep the footbath clean and mixed as the farm procedure states.
  • Work only in your own house or, if you must move, go from the youngest or cleanest flock to the oldest, never the other way.
  • Do not keep backyard chickens, pigeons or other birds at home. They can carry diseases such as Newcastle disease and avian influenza.
  • Keep wild birds and rodents out: close doors, fix holes in netting and clean up spilt feed.
  • Record every visitor and vehicle.

Daily checks

Walk through the house slowly at least at the start and end of each day, and more often in hot weather. Look, listen and smell:

  • Birds – Are they active and spread evenly? Signs of trouble include huddling, panting with open beaks, birds sitting alone with ruffled feathers, swollen heads, diarrhoea, coughing or sneezing.
  • Feed and water – Do all drinkers work? Are feeder lines running and full at feeding time?
  • Environment – Is the temperature right? Is the litter dry and loose, not wet and caked? Is there a smell of ammonia?
  • Equipment – fans, lights, nest boxes, alarms.

Remove dead birds at every walk and record them. Tell your supervisor immediately if deaths suddenly increase, if birds stop eating or drinking, or if egg production drops sharply. Some poultry diseases, like avian influenza, are controlled animal diseases under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported. Your manager and the vet will handle this, but your early warning is vital.

lessons.title: Feeding, body weight, lighting and males
lessons.html:
Controlled feeding

Modern breeder birds come from fast-growing lines. If they eat as much as they like, they become too fat. Fat breeders lay fewer eggs, and fat males mate poorly. So breeders get a measured amount of feed every day, according to the breeding company's management guide and the farm manager's plan.

  • Weigh the feed accurately. Do not give extra "because the birds look hungry".
  • Feed must spread fast so that every bird gets its share. Shy birds can miss out if the feeders fill slowly.
  • Males and females usually eat from separate feeders. Female feeders often have grills that stop the bigger-headed males from eating there, and male feeders are hung higher.
  • Make sure clean water is always available.

Weighing birds

Each week a sample of birds is weighed to check they follow the target weight curve. Catch birds gently from different parts of the house, weigh each on the scale and record the weight accurately. The manager uses these weights to decide how much feed to give and to check uniformity (how similar the birds are in weight). A good, even flock lays better.

Lighting programme

Light controls when hens start to lay and how well they keep laying. The manager sets a lighting programme with set hours of light each day. Your job is to:

  • Check the light clock or controller is working and set correctly.
  • Replace broken globes quickly.
  • Keep light-proof houses dark when they must be dark – close doors and fix light leaks.

Never change the lighting times yourself.

Caring for the males

Fertile eggs need healthy, active males. Watch males for poor feathers on the hens' backs (too many or rough males), lame males, males that are too thin or too fat, and males that do not mate. The manager decides how many males to keep per hen. Remove sick or lame males and report it, as instructed.

Handling birds

Handle birds calmly and gently. Hold a bird with both hands around the body, with the wings held against its sides. Never pick birds up by the neck, wings or one leg. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty to animals an offence.

lessons.title: Nests, hatching eggs and records
lessons.html:
Nest boxes

Hens should lay in the nests, not on the floor. Eggs laid on the floor are dirty, often cracked and carry more germs.

  • Keep nests clean, with dry nesting material (or clean mats in automatic nests).
  • Open nests before hens start to lay and close them at night if your farm does this, so birds do not sleep and dirty them.
  • Walk the house often in the morning to pick up floor eggs and gently move hens that are sitting in corners.

Collecting hatching eggs

Collect eggs several times a day, as your farm schedule states. Frequent collection keeps eggs clean, prevents cracks and stops eggs from warming up in the nest, which can start the embryo developing at the wrong time.

  1. Wash and sanitise your hands before you start.
  2. Handle eggs gently. Place each egg in the tray with the pointed end down and the blunt end, where the air cell is, up.
  3. Keep floor eggs separate from nest eggs and mark them. Your farm will decide if they can be set.
  4. Remove cracked, very dirty, very small, double-yolk or badly shaped eggs. These are rejects and must not go to the hatchery.
  5. Do not wash hatching eggs unless your farm procedure says so; washing the wrong way lets germs into the egg. Follow the farm's method for cleaning or fumigating eggs.

Storing hatching eggs

Take eggs to the egg room soon after collection. The egg room is kept cool and at a set humidity. Do not leave eggs in the sun or in a hot house passage. Stack trays carefully and label them with house, date and collection number.

Records

Accurate records tell the manager how the flock is doing. Record every day:

RecordWhy
Deaths and culls (male and female)Shows health problems early
Feed givenChecks the feeding plan
Water usedA drop can be the first sign of illness
Eggs: hatching, floor, rejectsShows production and egg quality
Temperatures, min and maxChecks the house climate

Key points

  • Parent stock produce hatching eggs, so their health affects many farms; follow biosecurity strictly.
  • Check birds, feed, water and equipment at every walk and report problems immediately.
  • Give the exact feed allowance and never change lighting times yourself.
  • Collect eggs often, gently, pointed end down, and keep floor eggs and rejects separate.
  • Keep accurate daily records of deaths, feed, water, eggs and temperatures.

quiz.question: What is the main product of a parent stock (breeder) flock?
Why are breeder birds given a measured amount of feed each day?

options.text: Because they do not like eating
To stop them getting too fat, which reduces egg production and mating

quiz.question: How should a hatching egg be placed in the tray?

options.text: Any way, it does not matter

quiz.question: Which practice helps keep disease out of a breeder farm?

options.text: Moving from the oldest flock to the youngest
Skipping the footbath when in a hurry
Showering in and changing into clean farm clothes

quiz.question: You notice birds suddenly stop drinking and more are dying. What should you do?

options.text: Wait a few days to see
